extracted.intended_audience: patent classification specialists, patent examiners, IP office staff and patent information professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for classifying and presenting patent documents in the International Patent Classification (IPC), including hierarchy, symbol presentation, references, definitions, and supplementary information. Intended to guide both assigning IPC symbols and using the IPC for searching and retrieval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of the IPC
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classification's primary purpose is the establishment of an effective search tool for retrieval of patent documents to establish novelty and evaluate inventive step/non-obviousness (including assessment of technical advance and useful results/utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional purposes include: (a) orderly arrangement of patent documents to facilitate access to technological and legal information; (b) basis for selective dissemination of information; (c) basis for investigating the state of the art; (d) basis for preparing industrial property statistics to assess technological development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official texts and languages
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classification is established in English and French, both texts being equally authentic; official texts in other languages may be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Internet version on the WIPO IPC website represents the official publication of the IPC and contains complete text of current and previous editions/versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of abbreviation on published documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The abbreviation 'Int.Cl.' may precede the classification symbols on published patent documents classified according to the Classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further details on presentation of symbols are provided in Section XII (presentation rules referenced elsewhere in the Guide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Layout: Hierarchical levels (section, class, subclass, group, subgroup)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPC is organised into hierarchical levels: sections (highest), classes, subclasses, groups (main groups) and subgroups (lower levels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each hierarchical level has specific symbol formats and titles (e.g., section symbol A–H; class symbol = section letter + two digits; subclass = class symbol + capital letter; group symbols = subclass + numbers/oblique stroke).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section: symbol and title usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Each section is designated by a capital letter A–H and has a section title to be considered a very broad indication of contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsections (informative headings without classification symbols) may exist within sections to group related subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class and class titles
rubrics_metrics.description: A class symbol consists of the section symbol followed by a two-digit number; class titles indicate content of the class; some classes have an index giving an informative summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: H01 ELECTRIC ELEMENTS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subclass symbol, title, index and guidance headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Subclass symbol = class symbol + capital letter; subclass title indicates precise content; many subclasses have an index and may include a guidance heading where a large part of the subclass relates to a common subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance headings (e.g., 'Volatile memory devices') indicate subject matter for a portion of the subclass and appear before the relevant groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group symbols, main groups and subgroups formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Group symbols consist of the subclass symbol followed by numbers separated by an oblique slash. Main group symbols end with '/00'; subgroups have at least two digits after the slash and are ordered as decimals relative to the main group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main group titles precisely define a field for search purposes and are presented in bold. Subgroup titles are indented and preceded by dots that show hierarchical position; their titles are read as dependent on higher-level titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete classification symbol composition
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete classification symbol comprises the combined symbols for section, class, subclass and the main group or subgroup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example layout illustrated in Guide: section (letter), class (2 digits), subclass (letter), group (e.g., 33/00 or 33/08).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPC is a hierarchical classification system: contents of lower levels are subdivisions of contents of higher levels to which they are subordinated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hierarchy is used to structure subject matter from broad (section) to specific (subgroup) for classification and searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy among subgroups determined by indentation (dots) not numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: The hierarchy among subgroups is determined solely by the number of dots (level of indentation) preceding their titles, and not by subgroup numbering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show that a three-digit three-dot subgroup may be hierarchically superior to a two-digit four-dot subgroup despite numbering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dots used to replace superior group titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Dots preceding a group title also stand in place of the titles of hierarchically superior groups to avoid repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits concise subgroup titles that implicitly include the wording of parent groups (example H01S 3/094).

rubrics_metrics.name: Option to classify in main groups only
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial property offices lacking sufficient expertise may choose to classify patent documents at the main group level only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This option exists to accommodate offices that cannot reliably assign detailed subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of groups: sequence principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups in each subclass are arranged to assist the user; for newer subclasses main groups generally proceed from the most complex/highly specialised subject matter to the least complex/least specialised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A residual main group (e.g., 99/00) is placed at the end of the scheme when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance headings usage
rubrics_metrics.description: When several successive main groups relate to common subject matter, a guidance heading (short underlined statement) may be placed before the first such main group to indicate the common subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The series covered extends to the next guidance heading or to a heavy line across the column. In exceptional cases, a guidance heading may cover a single main group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of titles: multipart titles and semicolons
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles may indicate content by single phrases or several related phrases linked together; if a title has two or more distinct parts separated by semicolons, each part should be interpreted as a separate title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multipart titles are used to treat distinct kinds of subject matter together when a single phrase is inconvenient. Examples provided (A42C 5/00; A41D 10/00).

rubrics_metrics.name: References: placement and basic role
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is a phrase in brackets referring to another place in the Classification, showing that the referenced subject matter is covered elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References are usually placed at the end of the title (or after the last part they relate to) and, when following a subclass or group title, relate to all hierarchically inferior places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of references — limiting references (scope-limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scope-limitation reference excludes specified subject matter from the scope of the place where it appears (even though it would otherwise be covered) and indicates where that excluded subject matter is classified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is critical for proper understanding and use of the place. In Definitions, scope-limitation references are listed under 'Limiting references'. Example given: A47B 25/00 excludes billiard tables (classified A63D 15/00).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of references — limiting references (precedence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A precedence reference states that another place 'takes precedence' when subject matter is classifiable in two places or different aspects are covered by different places; it is used so subject matter is classified in only one place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedence references occur most frequently at subgroup level and in Definitions they are listed under 'Limiting references'. They can act as scope-limitation or as classification rules for combination-type matters, depending on overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of references — non-limiting references (application-oriented)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application-oriented references point from function-oriented places to places where the subject matter is covered if specially adapted, used for a particular purpose, or incorporated in a larger system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: references from H01S (lasers) to eye surgery A61F 9/008, printers B41J 2/455, etc. In Definitions these are listed under 'Application-oriented references'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of references — non-limiting references (references out of residual places)
rubrics_metrics.description: References appearing in residual places (e.g., F21K 99/00) point to places that provide for the subject matter under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to guide searches when a residual catch-all group exists; listed in Definitions as 'References out of a residual place'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of references — non-limiting references (informative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informative references indicate the location of subject matter that is of interest for searching but is not within the scope of the place where the reference occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informative references often point from application-oriented places to function-oriented places and are listed in Definitions under 'Informative references'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting vs non-limiting references and their placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting references (scope-limitation and precedence) are included in classification schemes and Definitions; non-limiting references (application-oriented, out of residual place, informative) are progressively being removed from schemes and transferred to Definitions to improve readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users should consult Definitions for non-limiting references increasingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and interpretation of references: detailed rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules cover placement (end of title or after last relevant part), that references after a subclass/group relate to all inferior places, that quoted group may be the most relevant but other hierarchically related groups should be considered, and punctuation rules for multiple items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple items refer to same place they are separated by commas and the classification symbol given at the end; items referring to different places are separated by semicolons. Examples in Guide illustrate punctuation and grouping conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes: definition, scope and precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes define or explain specific words, phrases or the scope of places, or indicate how subject matter is classified; they may be associated with sections, subsections, classes, subclasses or groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes apply only to the places concerned and their subdivisions and override any general guidance in case of conflict. Information in notes associated with higher levels is also provided within subclass Definitions when affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of classification symbols cited in titles, references and notes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a symbol or contiguous range of symbols is cited, the citation comprises not just the symbols explicitly mentioned but their full set of hierarchically inferior subdivisions too (i.e., citation of a class includes its subclasses and their contents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPC does not use expressions like 'class and its subclasses' because citation already includes subordinate content. When a contiguous interval is indicated, the end is identified by the hierarchically highest symbol that covers the last intended group without including others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indication of changes vs previous editions/versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes relative to previous editions/versions are indicated by: italics for entries that are new, whose file scope has changed, or deleted; version indicators in square brackets showing edition/version where entry was new or modified; deleted group symbols appear with an italic indication of where subject matter was transferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple version indicators may be present; only the last is displayed by default with others accessible on demand (e.g., hover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Definitions for clarifying boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are recommended to clarify exact boundaries of classification places; they provide supplementary information but do not change the scope of classification entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions follow a structured format with a definition statement, explanation of limiting/informative references, interpretation of special classifying rules, and definitions of terms used in the place. Definitions are provided only for a limited number of subclasses/groups and will be expanded where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting references moved to Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting references indicating locations of subject matter of interest for searching are progressively introduced into Definitions rather than retained in schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change is intended to facilitate readability of the scheme while increasing useful related information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical structural formulae and graphic illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: In chemical areas, chemical structural formulae and graphic illustrations are introduced in the scheme or Definitions when necessary to define or interpret the scope of entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulae are introduced in the scheme for a limited number of entries when necessary (e.g., C07D 499/00); many additional formulae and graphics are available through hyperlinks in relevant classification entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard expressions: 'covered' / 'provided for'
rubrics_metrics.description: When subject matter is stated to be 'covered' by/in a classification place, it means the subject matter has characteristics enabling it to be classified in that place; 'provided for' has the same meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples referenced (e.g., group A41F 18/00; B60Q 11/00).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions indicating residual subject matter ('not otherwise provided for')
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'not otherwise provided for' in a group title means 'not provided for in any other group in the same subclass or in any other subclass'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of such expressions in a main group title does not expand the scope of the subclass beyond paragraph 69 (scope limits explained elsewhere). Residual main groups usually located at end of subclass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions for combination subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Main groups wording '… covered by more than one of main groups…' provide for subject matter consisting of combinations of characteristics not covered as a whole by a single specified group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some groups state '… not covered by any single one of main groups …' and may provide for combinations and subject matter not covered by other groups in the range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and use of 'i.e.' and 'e.g.'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'i.e.' has the sense of 'equals' and the two phrases joined are equivalent; 'e.g.' does not limit the sense of the preceding phrase but gives examples and may indicate typical illustration or matter included though no dependent subgroup provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given in the Guide demonstrate the distinct roles of 'i.e.' (definitional) and 'e.g.' (illustrative/inclusive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical connectors: 'A and B', 'A or B', 'either A or B, but not both'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A and B' requires the presence of both in same embodiment; 'A or B' implies A or B or both; 'either A or B, but not both' implies presence of only one of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These logical interpretations are to be applied when reading titles and group descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope vs file scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'scope' of a group is the subject matter covered by that classification place; the 'file scope' is the residual subject matter classified in the group itself but not in its subgroups. When a group has no subgroups, scope and file scope are identical; when new subgroups are added, group scope remains unchanged but its file scope is reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File scope is best understood as the residual matter classified in the group itself and is important for assigning documents when subgroups do not exist or are not applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary classification and obligatory classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary classification schemes provide symbols to be allocated in combination with symbols from other subclasses to enable complementary searching by cross-combination; they are not listed first when assigned to patent documents. Obligatory classification is the classification necessary to completely represent the invention information of a patent document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary classification symbols should be assigned in combination with primary classification symbols; examples and further rules are in the Guide (paragraphs referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting/presentation rules for schemes and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Main group symbols and titles are presented in bold; subgroup titles are preceded by dots indicating hierarchical level; subgroup ordering follows numeric-decimal ordering; titles may begin with capital letter if complete expression, or lower case if continuation of parent title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgroup titles must be read as dependent on the titles of groups under which they are indented; examples provided for correct reading and interpretation (e.g., 3/14 reads as 'Lasers characterised by the material used as the active medium').

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and listing conventions for references
rubrics_metrics.description: Where multiple items of subject matter are referred to the same place they are separated by a comma (symbol given at end); items referring to different places are separated by a semicolon and read independently; exception when a substantial part of wording is the same — common wording given once and different symbols separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in Guide illustrate comma vs semicolon usage and grouping to avoid repetition (e.g., A01B 77/00, E21B 10/42 examples).
